findings.quote: The trouble with investigating fires at sites where nobody is present.
findings.note: ARGUABLE: counsel's case — the unmanned-site problem is not a stray detail but the thread the piece ends on. Grendisham's whole objection is epistemic (“On an unmanned site at two in the morning, that is when somebody looked out of a window, not when anything caught”; “It looks late because nobody was there to see it early”), the writer concedes it stands (“Grendisham’s objection has not been answered, and it cannot be answered from files like these; it wants a probe inside a machine that later burns, and nobody has one”), and the closing sentence is that very scene (“with trucks waiting and no one there to watch?”). The case dies on the prompt delimiter “mainly”: paragraphs 1, 2 and 4 — the sixty-one-fire count, Calverend’s swabs and clock, and Tarrowfen’s date-sort onto the deduction schedule — have nothing to do with unmanned investigation, and only key D’s “familiar rule about which dryers burn, and a disputed account of why” covers all of them. Attractive but beatable.

findings.quote: She lays out the three positions and keeps her own counsel.
findings.note: ARGUABLE: counsel's case — the body is scrupulously attributed (“he says”, “she says”, “Tarrowfen says”), each of the three men is given his best argument, and the piece closes on an open question rather than a ruling (“What does an operator do at two in the morning on the eighth day of a wet harvest, with trucks waiting and no one there to watch?”), so a reader can claim the writer never rules. The case dies in the final paragraph, which is unattributed authorial judgment throughout: “The swabs are hard to walk past”, “nobody in the argument now defends it on the old ground”, “Grendisham’s objection has not been answered”, and — decisively for this prompt — “Calverend’s account fits the evidence without having been tested by it”, which is key C word for sense (old explanation dead, replacement untested). Attractive but beatable.

ARGUABLE: counsel's case — the setting supplies a strong pull toward footwear of the working kind (an allotment site; “a knee that will not manage the walk from the gate”), and the step-into-a-dead-man’s-position sense does attach to boots in modern usage, so an examinee can argue the variant is live. The case dies on the fixed form: the stem marks a set phrase (“The older hands have a phrase for this among themselves”) and the dictionary idiom is “waiting for dead men’s shoes” — key A. Nothing in the passage anchors either word, so the gap turns entirely on knowing the canonical form; adjudication should confirm the item accepts only “shoes”. Attractive but beatable.

findings.quote: The keepers stretched their opening hours in order to earn more of the hourly allowance.
findings.note: ARGUABLE (strongest case in the batch): counsel's case — the passage front-loads the incentive and rules out the alternative (“the keeper was allowed threepence for every hour the hatch stood open, and not a penny for the letters themselves”), records exactly the quantity that pays (“The quarterly returns recorded the hours and the letters”), and then shows the chandler buying seven extra hours for twenty-two extra letters (“the chandler's hatch opened at seven in the morning and took in 412 letters; the bookseller's opened at two and took in 390”). On those numbers the early opening earns money and collects almost nothing, which is what padding looks like. The case dies on the option’s own plural subject: the bookseller kept the shortest hours available to him (two in the afternoon until the eight o'clock cart), the opposite of stretching, so “the keepers” is false of one of the two; and “in order to” asserts a motive the passage never states — the only evaluative remark in the record finds nothing amiss (“The surveyor's note for that quarter remarked only that the chandler's flap wanted a new spring”). Key D needs no motive: the two hatches end at the same hour and take nearly the same count on very different openings. Attractive but beatable.

findings.quote: Eftersom anläggningarna var billiga att bygga kunde varje bygd förse sig själv med järn.
findings.note: ARGUABLE: counsel's case — the first clause is verbatim supported (“Ugnen kostade lera, sten och ved; den lagades eller revs och restes igen nästa höst”; “En blåsning gav några kilo järn och kunde göras av ett par karlar på ett dygn”), and the text does place production at parish level until the hytta arrives (“Först då flyttade tillverkningen från socknarna till bruken”), so a reader can take local self-supply for the text’s own point. The case dies on the universal “varje bygd”: the ore is not everywhere (“Långt ifrån varje mosse bär ett sådant skikt”, and those that do “bär det ojämnt”), yields varied sharply between sites half an hour’s walk apart, and the text nowhere claims a district met its own iron needs. Key D is the text’s own stated consequence (“Det är hantverkets utgångspunkt” … “Ur detta följer mycket av det som annars ser ut som fattigdom”). Attractive but beatable.

findings.quote: Hon anser frågan omöjlig att avgöra.
findings.note: ARGUABLE: counsel's case — the essay’s last movement is unresolved (“Ett par saker får jag ändå inte att gå ihop”), it names three loose ends (the four largest hemmansägare, the two widows, the overstrikes), and it says outright that the material cannot settle one of them (“överstrykningarna kan lika gärna vara ändrade beslut som rättelser av en felläsning – materialet svarar inte på det”). The case dies on the prompt’s scope, “sin egen misstanke”: the suspicion was that the association steered the words, and she disposes of it flatly one sentence earlier (“Ingen av mina tre mekanismer fanns alltså. Jag får ge Rämnestad rätt, och den förklaring som från början låg närmast är också den som står kvar”) — key B. What is left over is loose ends, not the question she set out to decide. Attractive but beatable.
